message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

**Verdict:** The pilot is a strong basis for the study, and the cost table is arithmetically correct. However, the study misreads its own pilot data on flats and uses a participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot. It also overlooks the fact that projected tonnage far exceeds Brookfield's contracted capacity. Once these are corrected, the "fully funded" conclusion no longer holds.

## 1. Flats did not "hold up": participation was 21% vs 66%

Table 1 shows houses at **66%** and flats at **21%**. That's less than a third of the house rate, not "broadly similar." This undermines a central recommendation, because the conclusion that one uniform service will work for flats isn't supported.

The data point the other way. Flats usually need a different approach, such as communal food waste bins, bin-store collection points or more targeted communication. That approach will carry its own costs, which aren't in the study.

## 2. The projection uses 64% participation, which comes from nowhere

The pilot's overall rate is **57%** (2,280 ÷ 4,000), and the pilot's 80/20 house/flat mix is the same as the district's. The 64% figure in section 3 doesn't match anything in Table 1.

**Corrected projection, using the pilot's own figures:**

| | Households | Participation | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% → 27,456 | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% → 2,184 | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | 57% | | **~2,870** |

The study's figure of 3,290 tonnes overstates tonnage by about **420 tonnes (15%)**. Applying the blended 1.9 kg to every household also slightly overstates the flats' yield.

## 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 notes that Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**, but the study then ignores it:
- Even the corrected tonnage is about **1,070 tonnes above capacity**. On the study's own figure, the excess is about 1,490 tonnes.
- The excess would have to go to the plant **46 miles away**. Its gate fee, the extra haulage, the crew time and any transfer arrangements are all uncosted.

The author's statement that "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is therefore true for only about 60% of the tonnage.

## 4. The disposal saving is overstated

The calculation works: £112 − £38 = £74 per tonne, and 3,290 t × £74 ≈ £243,000. On corrected tonnage the saving falls:
- **Corrected tonnage:** about 2,870 t × £74 ≈ **£212,000**. This assumes the overflow plant charges a similar gate fee and needs no extra transport, which is unlikely.
- **Brookfield's capacity only:** 1,800 t × £74 = **£133,200** is the secure saving.

## 5. The net cost no longer fits the funding

| | Study | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Gross cost | £733,400 | £733,400 |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ~£212,000 |
| **Net cost** | **£490,400** | **~£521,000** |
| Provisional funding | £520,000 | £520,000 |

The corrected net cost is already slightly **above** the allocation, before adding any of the missing costs below. The funding is also only **provisional** ("has indicated"), which the recommendation should treat as a risk, not a certainty.

## 6. "Every cost line is shown" — not quite

Each figure in Table 2 is correct:
- **Vehicles:** 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 ≈ £141,400.
- **Crews:** 12 × £34,000 = £408,000.
- **Total:** £733,400.

However, the following costs are missing:
- **Excess tonnage:** haulage and gate fees for the overflow plant.
- **Flats:** a separate approach, given the 21% participation.
- **Resilience:** a spare vehicle, and cover for crew holiday and sickness. Six vehicles and six crews leave no slack.
- **Management:** supervision and overheads.
- **Customer contact:** the dedicated phone line and web page described in section 6.
- **Start-up:** recruitment and training.
- **Vehicle financing:** the fleet needs about **£990,000 of capital** upfront. Depreciation spreads the cost but doesn't fund it, so the borrowing cost should be shown.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Pilot timing:** the pilot ran from January to June, so it covers no summer or autumn months and may reflect a novelty effect. The study should say whether participation changed over the six months.
- **Survey:** "81% of surveyed households" needs a sample size and response rate.
- **Timetable:** it has no contingency. Vehicles arrive in March for an April start, caddies go out to 52,000 households in the same month, and 12 operatives must be recruited from February. A short vehicle delay would push back the launch.

## What holds up

- The pilot design is good. It covered mixed wards and housing types and was measured weekly.
- The arithmetic in Table 1 and Table 2 is correct.
- Low contamination and positive feedback are real strengths.
- The gate-fee comparison method is sound, and the timetable logic of working back from vehicle lead time is sensible.

## Recommended changes before Cabinet

1. Correct section 2 to show that flats' participation was much lower, and propose and cost a specific approach for flats.
2. Base the projection on the pilot's actual rates, about 2,870 tonnes, and show a range.
3. Deal with the capacity gap: cost the overflow plant, negotiate more capacity at Brookfield, or phase the roll-out to match capacity until 2029.
4. Recalculate the saving and net cost, and add the missing cost lines and vehicle financing.
5. Present the funding as provisional, with a sensitivity showing the position if the allocation is lower.
6. Add contingency to the timetable.

The service is legally required, so the question isn't whether to proceed but how. As drafted, the study tells Cabinet the service is fully funded and suitable for a uniform roll-out, and its own data support neither claim.
